title: Why AI Matters Now
coreIdea: AI is becoming a new interface between people, knowledge and software.
keyLines: AI is changing how we interact with information and software.
In the past, we had to learn how software works.
Now software is starting to understand how we communicate.
Natural language is becoming a new user interface.
That makes digital capabilities accessible to many more people.
realCase: Think about finding information inside a company. Today, an employee may search SharePoint, open several documents, check emails and ask colleagues.
With AI, the interaction can become much simpler. The employee can describe the question in natural language, and AI can help find, summarize and connect the relevant information.
The important change is not just faster search. The user no longer needs to understand where every piece of information is stored.
discussionQuestion: Where in your daily work do you spend too much time finding information?
ending: Once AI understands what we want, the next question is how much work we want it to do for us.

title: Copilot vs Agent
coreIdea: A copilot helps you do the work. An agent can take responsibility for part of the work.
keyLines: A copilot usually works together with a human.
You ask, it responds, and you stay in control of every step.
An agent can work toward a goal across multiple steps.
It can use tools, make decisions and take actions.
The important difference is the level of delegation.
realCase: Imagine preparing a weekly project report.
A copilot can summarize documents when you ask.
An agent could collect the latest project information, identify important changes, prepare the report, and send it to you for review.
The key shift is from asking AI individual questions to giving AI a goal.
discussionQuestion: What part of your work would you feel comfortable delegating to an agent?
ending: If an agent can take responsibility for work, we need to understand what actually makes an agent possible.

title: What Makes an Agent?
coreIdea: An agent combines intelligence with context, tools, memory and boundaries.
keyLines: The model gives the agent intelligence.
Context tells the agent what is happening.
Tools allow the agent to interact with the outside world.
Memory helps it keep useful information over time.
Guardrails define what the agent is allowed to do.
realCase: Imagine an agent helping with customer requests.
The language model can understand the request.
Context gives it customer and product information.
Tools allow it to search a database or create a ticket.
Memory can preserve previous interactions.
Guardrails can require human approval before certain actions.
Together, these pieces turn a language model into a working system.
discussionQuestion: Which of these five elements do you think is hardest to build well in an enterprise?
ending: But having all these capabilities still does not guarantee reliable behavior. That is where the harness becomes important.

title: Agent Harness
coreIdea: The harness defines how an agent operates safely and reliably around the model.
keyLines: A powerful model does not automatically create a reliable agent.
The harness controls how the agent gets context and uses tools.
It defines permissions, approvals, error handling and evidence.
It also helps the agent understand when the task is complete.
The model provides intelligence. The harness provides discipline.
realCase: Imagine an agent updating an engineering document.
Writing new text is relatively easy.
The harder questions are different.
Which documents can it access?
Can it overwrite the original file?
Should it create a new version?
When does it need approval?
What happens when a tool fails?
How do we know what it changed?
These are harness questions.
discussionQuestion: If an AI agent could access your work systems tomorrow, what controls would you want around it?
ending: Some tasks need this kind of reasoning and control. Other tasks are much more predictable.

title: Workflow vs Agent
coreIdea: Use workflows for predictable paths and agents when the path depends on context.
keyLines: Workflows are strong when rules are clear.
Agents become useful when the next step depends on judgment.
Predictability is valuable.
Flexibility is also valuable.
The right architecture often combines both.
realCase: Consider an invoice approval process.
If every invoice follows the same approval rules, a workflow is usually enough.
Now imagine a supplier sends an unusual request with incomplete documents and several possible exceptions.
An agent can understand the situation and decide what information is missing.
A workflow can then execute the approved process reliably.
discussionQuestion: Which processes in your team are predictable, and which ones require real judgment?
ending: Whether we use a workflow or an agent, both depend heavily on the information we give them.

title: From Prompting to Context Engineering
coreIdea: Good AI results increasingly depend on good context.
keyLines: Prompting is useful, but it is only one part of the system.
AI needs the right information at the right time.
Good context can include documents, data, instructions and previous actions.
Poor context creates poor decisions.
Context engineering is becoming a core AI capability.
realCase: Suppose you ask AI to write a project status report.
A clever prompt may improve the writing.
But if the AI does not know the current schedule, open issues, decisions and latest changes, the report will still be weak.
The quality of the answer depends heavily on the quality of the context.
discussionQuestion: What information would AI need before it could really understand your work?
ending: Inside a company, some of the most valuable context comes from organizational knowledge.

title: Enterprise Knowledge
coreIdea: Enterprise AI becomes valuable when it can work with the knowledge people actually use.
keyLines: Companies already have huge amounts of knowledge.
The problem is that this knowledge is often fragmented.
It lives in documents, emails, databases and people’s experience.
AI can help connect these sources.
But the knowledge must still be accurate, accessible and governed.
realCase: Imagine a new engineer joining a project.
Important information may be spread across SharePoint, old reports, meeting notes, emails and senior engineers’ experience.
An AI assistant can help connect these sources and answer questions with relevant references.
This can reduce the time required to understand a project.
discussionQuestion: Where does the most valuable knowledge in your team currently live?
ending: Knowledge helps AI understand the situation. Tools allow AI to do something about it.

title: Tools and Actions
coreIdea: AI creates more value when it can move from answering questions to taking useful actions.
keyLines: A language model can generate information.
Tools allow it to interact with real systems.
It can search, create, update or trigger processes.
Every new tool increases capability.
Every new tool also increases responsibility and risk.
realCase: An employee asks an AI assistant about annual leave.
Answering the policy question is useful.
An agent connected to tools could also check the employee’s remaining leave, find available dates and prepare the leave request.
The experience moves from information to action.
discussionQuestion: Which system would create the most value if an AI agent could safely use it?
ending: As AI gains the ability to act, human judgment becomes even more important.

title: Human in the Loop
coreIdea: Human judgment should be placed at the moments where judgment creates the most value.
keyLines: Full automation is not always the goal.
Some decisions are low-risk and repetitive.
Others involve uncertainty, responsibility or business impact.
Humans should focus on these high-value decision points.
Good AI systems make escalation easy.
realCase: Imagine an AI agent preparing a technical change proposal.
It can collect information, compare versions and prepare the first draft.
But an experienced engineer may still approve the final technical decision.
AI handles much of the preparation.
The engineer focuses on judgment and accountability.
discussionQuestion: Which decisions in your work should always require human approval?
ending: Human approval helps with control, but people also need evidence before they can trust an AI recommendation.

title: Trust and Evidence
coreIdea: In enterprise AI, a useful answer also needs evidence.
keyLines: Confidence is not the same as correctness.
People need to understand where important information came from.
Good systems provide sources, logs and traceability.
Evidence allows humans to verify AI output.
Trust grows when the system makes verification easy.
realCase: Suppose AI tells an engineer that a component meets a technical requirement.
The statement alone is not enough.
The engineer wants to know which requirement, which document, which revision and which test result support that conclusion.
Evidence turns an AI answer into something that can be reviewed.
discussionQuestion: What evidence would you need before trusting an AI recommendation in your work?
ending: Evidence helps us understand what the agent did. Permissions determine what it is allowed to do.

title: Permissions and Governance
coreIdea: An agent should have only the authority required for its task.
keyLines: Agents can access information and take actions.
That makes permission design extremely important.
Access should follow the principle of least privilege.
Sensitive actions may require additional approval.
Governance should be part of the system from the beginning.
realCase: Imagine an HR agent helping employees with internal questions.
It may need access to general HR policies.
It should not automatically have access to every employee’s confidential information.
Different tasks require different levels of permission.
discussionQuestion: What information in your organization should an AI agent never access by default?
ending: Even with good permissions, we still need to know whether the AI system actually performs well.

title: AI Evaluation
coreIdea: We should evaluate AI as a system, not by one impressive demo.
keyLines: A good demo proves possibility.
Production requires consistency.
We should measure quality, reliability, cost and failure modes.
We should test normal cases and difficult cases.
Evaluation should continue after deployment.
realCase: An AI assistant may summarize one document perfectly during a demonstration.
But in production it may need to summarize thousands of documents from different departments.
Some may be incomplete, old or inconsistent.
The important question is how well the system performs across the full range of real situations.
discussionQuestion: How would you decide whether an AI use case is good enough for production?
ending: Before we evaluate an AI solution, we first need to choose the right problem to solve.

title: Finding Good AI Use Cases
coreIdea: The best AI opportunities often begin with business friction.
keyLines: Start by looking for wasted time and repeated effort.
Look for searching, reading, comparing and summarizing.
Look for handovers and waiting time.
Look for work that depends on scattered information.
Then ask whether AI can remove some of that friction.
realCase: A project manager spends several hours every week collecting updates from different teams.
The information already exists, but it is spread across emails, documents and systems.
AI could collect the information, identify changes and prepare a first summary.
This is a strong use case because the pain already exists.
discussionQuestion: What repetitive task would you happily never do manually again?
ending: Once we find a good task, the next opportunity is often to look beyond that single task.

title: From Task to Workflow
coreIdea: The biggest AI value often comes from redesigning the workflow around AI.
keyLines: Many people start with individual AI tasks.
That is a useful first step.
Bigger value appears when we connect multiple steps.
We should look at the complete flow of information and decisions.
AI gives us a reason to rethink how work is organized.
realCase: Imagine creating a test report.
First, AI helps write one paragraph.
Later, the process can grow.
AI finds previous reports, extracts product information, identifies relevant standards, generates the first draft and prepares the document for review.
The value comes from connecting the complete workflow.
discussionQuestion: Which AI use case in your team could grow from one task into an end-to-end workflow?
ending: Microsoft is building several tools around exactly this kind of work.

title: Microsoft 365 Copilot
coreIdea: Microsoft 365 Copilot brings AI into the tools where employees already work.
keyLines: Most employees already spend their day in Microsoft 365.
Copilot brings AI into Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams.
This reduces the need to move between tools.
The real advantage is access to work context.
Adoption becomes easier when AI appears inside familiar workflows.
realCase: After a long project meeting, an employee may need to review notes, identify decisions and prepare follow-up actions.
Copilot can help summarize the meeting and prepare a first draft of the follow-up.
The user remains inside the same work environment.
discussionQuestion: Which Microsoft 365 application would benefit most from AI in your daily work?
ending: Personal productivity is one layer. Companies also need agents designed for specific business purposes.

title: Copilot Studio
coreIdea: Copilot Studio helps organizations create agents around specific business needs.
keyLines: General AI cannot know every business process.
Purpose-built agents can combine instructions, knowledge and tools.
They can connect AI with enterprise systems.
They can also include business rules and approval steps.
This makes agents more relevant to specific teams.
realCase: Imagine an internal engineering support agent.
It understands engineering guidelines, searches approved documents, answers common questions and directs unusual cases to the right expert.
The agent has a clear business purpose and a controlled knowledge scope.
discussionQuestion: If your team could build one specialized agent, what job would you give it?
ending: Many actions behind that agent still need predictable execution. This is where Power Automate fits well.

title: Power Automate
coreIdea: Power Automate provides predictable execution for repeatable business processes.
keyLines: Many business processes follow clear rules.
These processes do not always need AI reasoning.
Power Automate can connect systems and execute defined steps.
It is especially useful for approvals, notifications and data movement.
Agents and automation can work together.
realCase: An agent receives a customer request and decides that manager approval is required.
The agent does not need to invent the approval process.
Power Automate can start the predefined approval flow, collect the decision and return the result.
Reasoning and execution have different roles.
discussionQuestion: Which manual approval or notification process in your team could already be automated today?
ending: Processes also need places where people can see, edit and manage structured information.

title: Power Apps and Dataverse
coreIdea: AI still needs structured data, clear state and good human interfaces.
keyLines: Conversations are useful, but not every task should live inside a chat.
Business processes often need forms, tables and status tracking.
Power Apps provides user interfaces.
Dataverse can provide structured business data.
Together they create a stable environment around AI.
realCase: Imagine an AI agent identifying potential quality issues.
Employees still need a place to review each issue, assign an owner, change its status and record the final decision.
A Power App can provide that workspace.
AI supports the process while structured systems preserve the business state.
discussionQuestion: Which part of your work still needs a structured screen even if AI becomes much more powerful?
ending: This leads to one of the most useful enterprise patterns: combining agents with the Power Platform.

title: Agent + Power Platform
coreIdea: Let agents handle ambiguity and let automation handle predictable execution.
keyLines: Agents are strong at understanding messy situations.
Workflows are strong at executing defined processes.
Apps provide structured human interaction.
Data platforms provide shared business state.
Combining these capabilities creates stronger enterprise solutions.
realCase: Imagine a supplier sends an unusual technical request by email.
An agent reads the message, understands the request and identifies the required process.
Power Automate starts the correct workflow.
Dataverse stores the case.
A Power App allows engineers to review it.
The agent handles ambiguity while the platform provides structure.
discussionQuestion: Where could your team combine AI reasoning with an existing Power Platform process?
ending: Technology provides the capability. Someone still needs to connect these possibilities with real business problems.

title: The Role of an AI Champion
coreIdea: An AI Champion connects technological possibilities with real business problems.
keyLines: AI Champions do not need to have every technical answer.
Their value comes from connecting people, problems and possibilities.
They help teams identify useful experiments.
They also help people understand both opportunities and limitations.
Good AI adoption spreads through people who can translate technology into everyday work.
realCase: A colleague says, “I spend hours every week preparing this report.”
An AI Champion does not immediately recommend a product.
First, they understand the workflow.
Where does the information come from?
Which steps require judgment?
Which parts are repetitive?
What risks exist?
Only then do they explore whether Copilot, an agent or Power Platform can help.
discussionQuestion: What is one problem in your team that you would like to explore with AI?
ending: The most important question is no longer what AI can do. The useful question is where AI can make our work meaningfully better.
